Taco Time Hot Sauce Recipe    Ingredients: - 1/4 cup of Water   - 1/2 cup of Dried Arbol Peppers   - 1 tablespoon of Fresh Cilantro, Chopped   - 1/2 cup of Distilled White Vinegar   - 1/4 teaspoon of Chili Powder   - Salt to Taste   - Freshly Ground Black Pepper to Taste   - 1/4 teaspoon of Freshly Ground Cumin Powder   - 1/2 cup of Shredded Carrots   - 3/4 cup of Diced Red Bell Pepper   - 1/2 cup of Minced White Onion   - 1/2 stalk of Medium Celery   Instructions: 1. Remove the stems from the dried arbol peppers and toast them in a dry skillet over medium heat for about 2 minutes until fragrant    2. In a heatproof bowl, pour boiling water over the toasted peppers, covering them completely, and let them soak for 15-20 minutes until softened   3. Drain the soaked peppers and transfer them to a blender with fresh cilantro, red bell pepper, white onion, and celery, blending until smooth   4. Pour the blended mixture into a saucepan and add distilled white vinegar, water, chili powder, salt, black pepper, and cumin, stirring well to combine   5. Bring the mixture to a boil over medium heat, then reduce the heat and let it simmer for 20-25 minutes, stirring occasionally until slightly thickened   6. Taste and adjust the seasonings as needed by adding more chili powder for spice or more vinegar for tanginess

A lot of couples try to open right after an affair, and not because they're ready, but because the disconnection feels unbearable. And here's what doesn't work. Opening before repair, because it usually doesn't fix the rupture. It spreads it. So what helps instead? Slow down, rebuild trust, and create real stability first. Because opening doesn't remove the hurt underneath. It just gives the hurt more places to show up.

And I think what makes this work really well is the love interests are so different, but we immediately see why the protagonist would be equally attracted to them. You keep hearing people say, “I just want to take things slow.” And on the surface, that sounds healthy. No rushing. No chaos. No jumping in too fast. That’s what people are calling “slow dating.” And in theory, it’s a good thing. But here’s what’s actually happening for a lot of people…it’s not slow dating. It’s stalled dating. Research around modern relationships—even data reflected in places like the Pew Research Center—shows people are more cautious than ever. More guarded. More hesitant to invest. And part of that is understandable. People have been hurt. They’ve been burned. So they say, “Let’s go slow.” But psychology has shown something important for a long time. Human beings don’t just need safety—they need movement. That’s part of what Edward Deci and Richard Ryan talked about with motivation. We need a sense of progress. Forward motion. If something just sits in uncertainty too long, it doesn’t feel safe…it starts to feel confusing. So what happens? You get situations where there’s texting, talking, maybe even seeing each other…but no real direction. No clarity. No decision. And people call that “taking it slow.” But it’s not. It’s avoidance dressed up as patience. And here’s the problem. When there’s no direction, your mind fills in the gaps. You start overthinking. You start trying to read signals. You start investing emotionally without actually knowing where you stand. And that creates anxiety—not stability. Because real slow dating isn’t about dragging things out. It’s about being intentional while you move forward. It’s clarity with pacing. Not confusion with time. You can take things slow and still be clear. You can take things slow and still say, “This is what I’m looking for.” You can take things slow and still evaluate whether someone is actually showing up consistently. Slow doesn’t mean passive. And that’s where a lot of people are getting stuck right now. They think they’re doing something healthy…but they’re actually sitting in uncertainty and calling it progress. And if you’re honest, you’ve probably felt that. You’ve been in something that just hovered. No commitment, no clarity, just enough connection to keep you there. That’s not slow dating. That’s delayed decision-making. And if you’re sitting there thinking, “Okay…so how do I actually do this the right way?”—that’s exactly why I built the resources in my Stanstore. Not to rush you into anything, but to help you stay grounded, see what’s actually happening, and make clear decisions instead of drifting. Because this is where the shift happens. You don’t need to move faster. You need to move clearer. Because if you don’t, you won’t just waste time…you’ll invest emotionally in something that was never actually moving forward. #healing #healingjourney #dating #date #selfrespect

Instead of jumping in and trying to prove yourself right away, it's important to watch and listen first. Sometimes people are eager to make changes in their new roles, especially when starting a managerial or leadership position. But even well-intentioned changes can do more harm than good. Before you suggest workflow and process changes, understand why something happens the way it does. Even when ideas are solid, teams can feel blindsided, especially when you haven't taken time to understand why something happens a certain way. Treating roles outside leadership poorly will damage your reputation. Administrative support, coordinators, and other operational professionals are often quiet leaders within organizations. These staff members hold critical knowledge and influence, and how you treat them speaks about your professionalism. There are ways that you can develop professional relationships without centering them around gossip or negative conversations. Don't harm your personal brand by doing it just because others are. Whether you're working from home or in the office, it's important to put your best foot forward. This includes dressing appropriately for video calls, joining with enough time to set up your workspace, and arriving and leaving on time. When starting a new role, it's natural to compare your new environment to your previous one. However,  it's best to avoid making these comparisons out loud. Your employer hired you to share your expertise and opinions, but ensure it's the right time to do so. It's best to frame suggestions in terms of your current organization's goals and explain why you believe something will or won't work to avoid coming across as overly critical. Build a rapport with those around you first, and then reprimand in private. No matter what level role you're in, don't be afraid to ask for help or support. Whether you have questions about the ins and outs of your specific role or the company culture, it's important to ask questions and lean on the resources available to you. When it comes to using shared resources in the office, you should never assume it's one person's job to replace and replenish them. In the ancient pictographic sense, HER represents the House of Babel, a system of "Confusion" that functions as a false mother attempting to nurture the children of Yasharael with the milk of rebellion and lawlessness. She is the physical and spiritual embodiment of a world structure that consumes the seed of the covenant through deception, labor, and the erasure of the Father’s true Name and Torah. To "come out of her" is a direct command to sever the umbilical cord to this dying system and return to the original authority of Yahuah. In Dabarym (Deuteronomy) 28:68, Yahuah warns that if the Torah is not guarded, the people will be brought into Mitsraym (a place of narrowness or bondage) again with ships. The text states, "And there ye shall be sold unto your enemies for bondmen and bondwomen, and no man shall buy you." In the ancient context, "buy" often translates to "redeem" or "save," meaning that while the people were sold into a physical and mental state of servitude, no human power or earthly nation would be able to snatch them out of that hand until the appointed time of the Father. ​This theme of being scattered among all people, from one end of the earth even unto the other, is further established in Dabarym 28:64. It describes a state where the remnant would serve other mighty ones—wood and stone—which neither they nor their fathers had known. This scattering was not a random act of history but a purposeful "sifting" mentioned in Amus (Amos) 9:9. Yahuah says, "For, lo, I will command, and I will sift the house of Yasharael among all nations, like as corn is sifted in a sieve, yet shall not the least grain fall upon the earth." This confirms that even while being sold and scattered, the seed is preserved and never truly "lost" from His sight. ​Furthermore, YashYahu (Isaiah) 11:11-12 speaks to the second gathering, where Yahuah shall set His hand again the second time to recover the remnant of His people from the lands where they were driven. It mentions the "outcasts of Yasharael" and the "dispersed of Yahudah" from the four corners of the earth. These passages emphasize that the "scattering" was a branded mark of the identity of the true children, serving as a reminder that their current state was predicted long ago. ​When we look at these scriptures through the lens of the ancient paths, we see a people who are "sold" into systems of confusion but are "not caught" in the sense that their true spirit and covenant identity remain anchored in the Father's plan. Crockpot Turkey Chili Ingredients 1 tbsp vegetable oil 1 yellow onion, chopped 1 red bell pepper, chopped 2 lb ground turkey 3 garlic cloves, minced 1/4 cup tomato paste 2 cans (14.5 oz) fire roasted tomatoes 1 can (15 oz) black beans, drained and rinsed 1 can (15 oz) kidney beans, drained and rinsed 1 cup frozen corn kernels ¼ Cup diced green chilies 1 1/2 cups chicken broth 2 tsp chili powder 1 tsp ground cumin 1 tsp dried oregano 1/2 tsp salt 1/2 tsp black pepper Shredded pepper jack, diced avocado, corn chips for serving Method 1. Heat oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Cook onion and bell pepper until softened, 8-10 minutes. Add turkey and cook through, 6-8 minutes. Stir in garlic and tomato paste and cook 2 minutes. 2. Transfer to a slow cooker. Add tomatoes with their juices, both beans, corn, broth, and all seasonings. Stir to combine. Cook on high for 4 hours or low for 6 hours. 3. Use an immersion blender to pulse the chili a few times directly in the pot until slightly thickened but still chunky. Alternatively, remove about 2 cups of chili, blend until smooth, and stir back in. 4. Serve with pepper jack, avocado, and corn chips. #CrockpotTurkeyChili

What tool loadout would I recommend for an electrician apprentice just getting into the trades? A backpack tool bag, and high quality essentials. So what would I recommend for any apprentice? Definitely a backpack style tool bag, no matter which brand you get. This is the Carhartt one. I think they. I think it's called the Station Bag. But whatever brand you get, I would recommend finding out if it has a hard bottom like this. This is also modular, so it has these little couches with clips on them that go onto this back section here. So you can literally outfit the inside as you see fit. So the first thing is a good pair of lineman pliers. You don't have to get fancy. Want restaurant quality at home in under 30 minutes? 🤩🤌Then you’ll love this dish! PACCHERI ALLA VITTORIO is a robust Italian pasta dish with a velvety smooth tomato sauce. This is the slightly easier, quicker version than an earlier video I did using several kinds of tomatoes in this dish. This version uses sweet cherry tomatoes which are also less acidic 🍅 I used a @USER Whole Wheat Paccheri in this dish. But you can use traditional Paccheri shaped pasta or rigatoni if you can’t find Paccheri 🍝 Completely dairy free and vegan and full of plant protein, you will love this creamy sauce that feels decadent! And don’t forget to “fare la scarpetta”! Which translates to mopping up the leftover sauce with bread!🥖 Paccheri alla Vittorio🍅 Ingredients 1 pint of fresh cherry or grape tomatoes 4 cloves garlic 2 tablespoons olive oil sea salt to taste 1/2 cup cooked white beans 1 cup water 1/2 lb of paccheri (you can use rigatoni if you can't find paccheri) fresh basil leaves Directions Cut all of the cherry tomatoes in half. Peel and thinly slice the garlic and set aside. Add the olive oil to a large sauté pan or stockpot on medium/high heat. Add in all of the tomatoes and garlic to the pan or pot. Then add in the salt and stir. Add in the beans and then the water. Cook until everything is softened, about 10-15 minutes. You can put a lid on the pan to help with the cooking. While the sauce is cooking, bring a pot of water to a boil and then add in the paccheri. Cook on the al dente side of the package instructions. Using a high speed blender, pour the ingredients into the blender, and while holding the lid down carefully, blend until smooth. Bring the sauce back to the pan. Drain the pasta; then add the pasta to the sauce. Coat the paccheri with the sauce. Garnish with basil leaves. Serve warm. Mangiamo! #easyrecipe #healthymeals

Authentic guacamole is celebrated for its simplicity, relying on high-quality, fresh ingredients to let the creamy avocado shine. While variations exist across different regions and households in Mexico, the core philosophy is always the same: keep it fresh and don't over-process the ingredients. ### Traditional Ingredients  * **Ripe Avocados:** The foundation. Look for Hass avocados that are slightly soft to the touch but not mushy.  * **Onion:** Finely diced. White onion is most traditional for its sharp, clean bite, though red onion is commonly used for a milder flavor and pop of color.  * **Fresh Cilantro:** Essential for that characteristic herbaceous freshness.  * **Chiles:** Serrano peppers are the traditional choice for a clean, sharp heat, though jalapeños are a widely accepted and excellent substitute.  * **Salt:** Essential to tie the flavors together. Kosher or sea salt works best.  * **Lime Juice (Optional but popular):** Used to brighten the flavor and help prevent oxidation (browning). *Note: While many versions include tomatoes and garlic, purists often omit them, arguing that they can mask the delicate flavor of the avocado. If you do include them, ensure the tomatoes are seeded and finely diced to avoid a watery texture.* ### The Authentic Method: Using a Molcajete For the most authentic texture and flavor, a **molcajete** (a traditional Mexican stone mortar and pestle) is used to grind the ingredients. This process releases the aromatic oils from the chiles, cilantro, and onion before the avocado is introduced, creating a deeper, more cohesive flavor profile.  1. **Prepare the Base:** Place the diced onion, chile, cilantro, and a pinch of salt into the molcajete. Use the *tejolote* (the pestle) to grind these ingredients into a coarse paste.  2. **Add Avocado:** Add the flesh of the avocados to the mixture.  3. **Mash:** Gently mash the avocado with the pestle. You are looking for a rustic, chunky consistency—avoid turning it into a completely smooth puree.  4. **Season:** Fold in the lime juice and adjust the salt to taste. Serve immediately while fresh. ### Tips for Success  * **Don't Over-Mash:** The best guacamole has texture. A few chunks of avocado provide a better mouthfeel than a completely smooth dip.  * **Temperature Matters:** Serve at room temperature for the best flavor; refrigeration can mute the nuance of the avocado.  * **Fresh is Best:** Because avocado oxidizes quickly, guacamole is best made just before serving. If you must prepare it ahead of time, press a piece of plastic wrap directly onto the surface of the guacamole to minimize air exposure.  * **The "Pit" Myth:** Placing the avocado pit in the bowl is a popular trick, but it is largely ineffective at preventing browning. It only protects the specific area of avocado it is physically touching. Lime juice and plastic wrap are much more effective. The Architecture of a Server The genius of Discord lies in its hierarchy. Unlike the "feed" based nature of X or Facebook, Discord is organized into Servers, which are essentially private or public mansions with different "rooms" called Channels. Text Channels: These are the backbone of the platform, supporting Markdown for formatting and hosting everything from casual memes to complex technical documentation. Voice & Video: Using the WebRTC protocol, Discord provides low-latency voice chat. The "hangout" vibe is perfected here; you don't "call" someone, you simply sit in a room, and others can drop in to join you. Categories & Roles: This is where the community management magic happens. Roles allow for complex permission systems, giving users specific colors, badges, and access levels. The Nitro Experience While Discord is free, the "Nitro" subscription is what unlocks the power user features. This brings us to the 4,000-character limit. While standard users are capped at 2,000 characters per message to prevent spam and keep chats readable, Nitro users get double that. This is essential for: Roleplayers: Who often write long, descriptive "posts" to move a story forward. Server Owners: Who need to post massive, detailed rule sets or announcements in a single block. Developers: Who might be pasting large snippets of code. Beyond the text limit, Nitro provides higher-quality video streaming (4K/60fps), massive file upload limits (up to 500MB), and the ability to use "Global Emojis"—taking your custom server emojis into your friend's DMs. From Gaming to Everything The 2020 pandemic was the turning point for Discord. It moved from being "Chat for Gamers" to "Your Place to Talk." Suddenly, the platform was flooded with knitting circles, AI art collectives, local neighborhoods, and even corporate teams tired of the "stiffness" of Slack. This shift forced Discord to refine its safety tools. Features like AutoMod and the Safety Center became paramount to protect the 150+ million monthly active users from raids and spam. It has become the infrastructure of the modern internet—a place where you don't just consume content, but where you actually live your digital life. Whether you are a casual user sending a "gg" after a match or a Nitro subscriber utilizing every bit of your 4,000-character allowance to coordinate a 200-person raid, Discord has redefined how we stay connected in an increasingly digital world. Nobody believed her. That was the part that cut deepest. In 1941, Mary Jane Ward was thirty-five years old, a married novelist trying to build something real in New York City. She had already published books. She had a husband who loved her, a life she was carefully constructing word by word. Then her mind began to fracture — slowly at first, then all at once. Anxiety spiraled into sleeplessness. Sleeplessness collapsed into delusion. And before she fully understood what was happening, she was no longer in control of anything. Doctors examined her. Signed the papers. And her husband, believing he was doing the right thing, watched them take her away. Rockland State Hospital was described to him as a peaceful place. Green lawns. Fresh air. Quiet recovery. What he did not know was that the moment his wife passed through those doors, she would cease to exist as a person and become simply a patient. A number. A problem to be managed. They took her suitcase. Her wedding ring. Even her hairpins. Then they placed her in a ward crowded with dozens of women and told her nothing about what came next. What came next was not peace. Patients were pulled from their beds before dawn. They scrubbed floors with lye soap that burned their skin raw. They sat for hours on hard benches in silence, forbidden from crying, forbidden from protesting, forbidden from asking when they could go home. Any resistance was noted. Any emotion was treated as evidence of deeper illness. The system had arranged itself so that objecting to your treatment could be used to justify more of it. The worst was the electroshock machine. There was no anesthesia. No muscle relaxants. Only leather straps, a rubber block between the teeth, and a current powerful enough to erase entire sections of memory. Mary Jane woke from one session unable to remember her own age. She asked a nurse what day it was. The nurse said nothing and wrote on a clipboard instead. Another woman might have shattered. Mary Jane began to watch. She had spent years training herself to observe the world carefully enough to put it into words. Now she turned that same attention on everything around her — the hierarchy of the wards, the way attendants rewarded silence and punished questions, the sound of nurses' shoes on linoleum at night, the way doctors avoided meeting patients' eyes. She was still a writer, even here. Especially here. She memorized what she witnessed with the quiet discipline of someone who intended to survive long enough to use it. Eight and a half months after she arrived, the hospital declared her improved and released her. They had lost her belongings, so she walked out wearing someone else's clothes. It took nearly three years to fully recover her memory. Then she sat down and wrote. The novel she produced, published in 1946 under the title The Snake Pit, was officially presented as fiction. Readers knew otherwise. The cold baths, the locked wards, the shock treatments, the maddening arbitrariness of institutional power — it rang true in a way invented stories rarely do. The book became an immediate bestseller, condensed by Reader's Digest, chosen as a Book of the Month, and within two years adapted into a major Hollywood film starring Olivia de Havilland. But the real impact was not on bookstore shelves. Journalists began investigating psychiatric institutions across the country. Lawmakers started asking questions that had never been asked publicly before. States began examining their own mental health laws, limiting restraints, changing how patients could be committed against their will. One woman's careful observations from inside a locked ward had become the spark for a national reckoning. Mary Jane Ward died in 1981. Most people today would not recognize her name. She never organized a movement or delivered speeches from a stage. She did something quieter and far more dangerous to a system built on silence. She paid attention. She remembered. And she made sure the world could not look away. Some people are broken by what the world puts them through. Mary Jane Ward took notes. #MaryJaneWard #TheSnakePit #SheWroteItAnyway

After Calcination burns away the false — comes Dissolution. In classical alchemy, the alchemist would take the ash left behind by the fire — and submerge it in water. Dissolving what remained. Breaking down the structure further. Until nothing solid was left. Just particles. Suspended. In flux. This is also what happens in the second stage of inner transformation. And it is the stage most people mistake for breakdown. What Dissolution looks like in real life: The emotional walls you built to keep yourself safe — begin to soften. The carefully constructed defences — the numbness, the busyness, the control — start to lose their hold. Things you thought you had dealt with begin to surface. Old grief. Old anger. Old fear. Rising up from places you thought were sealed. You may find yourself crying without knowing why. Feeling more sensitive than usual. More raw. More permeable. Like something that was frozen is beginning to thaw. What Dissolution feels like: Unsteady. Like the ground you were standing on has become water. Like the identity you rebuilt after Calcination isn’t as solid as you thought. The ego — which survived the fire — now finds itself without the structure it usually relies on. And it experiences this as threat. As chaos. As something going terribly wrong. Why Dissolution is essential: Because the structures that dissolved were the ones keeping you from accessing what was beneath them. The emotional armour. The inherited beliefs. The survival patterns so deeply embedded you stopped seeing them as patterns and started seeing them as personality. Dissolution doesn’t destroy you. It returns you to a state of openness — of genuine receptivity — that makes the next stages of transformation actually possible. In mental transmutation — Dissolution is the practice of allowing the emotions that surface to move through you rather than pushing them back down. It is learning to be in the water without drowning in it. To feel without being consumed. The Idea We Want to Believe "Everyone is good deep down." It's a comforting thought. We teach it to kids, we repeat it after tragedies, we want it to be true because the alternative is messier. If not everyone has a good heart, then the world requires vigilance, boundaries, and sometimes, disappointment.  But reality doesn't care about comfort. Observing history, relationships, workplaces, and even families shows a different pattern: most people have some mix of good and bad motives, and a minority operate with little regard for others unless it benefits them. "Not everybody has a good heart" isn't a cynical take. It's a practical one. 2. What "Good Heart" Actually Means Let's define terms before we go further. Having a "good heart" usually means: - *Empathy*: You can feel and care about others' pain without it directly affecting you. - *Consistency*: You act with integrity when no one is watching. - *Altruism*: You're willing to give time, money, or effort with no expected return. - *Restraint*: You don't exploit people even when you have the power to do so. Notice this isn't about never making mistakes. People with good hearts mess up, get angry, act selfishly sometimes. The difference is in the default setting and the willingness to correct course. Someone without a good heart lacks that default. Their default is self-interest, and empathy is either absent or switched on only when useful. 3. Why This Is True: Three Forces at Work *A. Evolution and Self-Preservation*   Humans evolved in small groups where cooperation increased survival. But cooperation only works if it's not one-sided. Cheating, lying, and free-riding are also evolutionary strategies. If you can take resources without giving back, you gain an advantage. That's why every society has had to invent rules, shame, and punishment. If everyone had a good heart, we wouldn't need laws, contracts, or locks. *B. Environment and Incentives*   People aren't fixed. A person with a decent heart can act badly if the system rewards it. Think of a salesperson paid only on commission who starts lying to customers. Think of a politician who starts out idealistic and learns that compromise and manipulation get more done. The heart doesn't change overnight, but incentives shape behavior fast. Conversely, a person with selfish tendencies can act well when the cost of being caught is high. This is why institutions matter more than vibes. *C. Personality and Upbringing*   Psychology research on traits like the "Dark Triad" - narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy - shows that some people score high on callousness and manipulation. These aren't always serial killers. They're often high-functioning people in business, media, and politics. Upbringing also matters: neglect, abuse, and modeling of exploitation teach kids that the world is hostile and the only safe move is to take before you're taken from. You can change, but it takes work most people never do. 4. How It Shows Up in Real Life You don't need to look far: *In relationships*: The person who is charming at first, love-bombs you, then isolates and controls you. They had a heart that worked for them, not for you.  *In work*: The colleague who takes credit for your work, sabotages you quietly, and smiles in meetings. Their heart is aligned with their status, not fairness. *In business*: Companies that sell products they know are harmful because profit outweighs harm. The boy peeks furtively from the volume of his mother's skirts, scrubbing at his tears with tiny fists clad in black cotton gloves. 

"Maman, I cannot bear to see him!" 

"Hush, my little chick– Monsieur, my apologies for my son… he has never…" 

"Beheld the beloved dead," the man from the pulpit says, matter-of-fact, and nods, "If I may…?" 

With a small gesture of her hand, the mother consents, and gently separates from the boy, who stands brave and puffy-eyed before the tall man, eyes screwed to the floor as he sniffles. The man, with apparent difficulty, lowers himself to kneel on one knee– you can see the primal expression of pain pinching his features even from your vantage point– and talks to the boy, soft and low and lulling, so low that you cannot hear as the two speak and the man gently clasps the boy's hands. 

There has been a stony cast to the man's demeanor until this moment, when he softens a mote imperceptibly, and you silently slip nearer, choosing a shadowy alcove in which to ensconce yourself to view the tableau better, a story unfolding before your eyes. 

"It is good, I think, to say goodbye to those you love. And your love held him dearest in your heart, I take it?" The man asks the boy.
- The boy nods wordlessly, sniffling, scrubbing at his eyes again. They are the color of cerulean; oft considered a mark of luck in Ishgard, to have such a shade of blue in the eyes. Azure. Fortuitous portent found in this boy who struggles to confront the finality of death. You hang your head, watching them through your lashes. 

"In my work," The man says softly, taking the boy gently by the shoulders, "I could hardly gainsay I have loved him as gently as you; I have bathed him, shaved his face carefully, dressed him meticulously to ready him for this goodbye. There is naught to fear in the company of the departed; naught else but the enormity of one's own grief. Your mother tells me it is your ambition to become a Knight Dragoon, is that correct?"

The boy, face reddened, nods profusely and stammers a "Yes," little fists clenched at his sides, in the woolen fabric of his little black hose. 

"Allow yourself this first victory over Death, beloved," The man says, "And I will be as your seneschal." 

He extends his hand, and the child after some small hesitation takes it. They walk together to the casket, hand in hand.

"No way to address the grieved, Ser," you say. For all his poise and the unflinching patience he'd shown that toddling child not even a bell ago (even if still a bit terse), he is rude, as if your presence is no more than an intrusion on a strictly regimented plan. Your next word would blow a house of cards down, and he is cross for it. 

Gaze still pinned on the crowd, he squints a little, minute lines at the corners of his eyes betray an exhaustion surely beyond his years, and he leans toward you casually, his fougere of deepwood fern, resinous, spicy and slightly acrid wafts into your nose, your mouth, "You lie," his caustic tone belies his placid expression and he gives a wave and a nod at a departing mourner who gives him a sad smile and leaves, sniffling into her handkerchief, "You are not of the grieved. 11. Serve warmed in the oven and sprinkled with icing sugar.
